name: Ben Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. This interview is confidential. What fills your working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Ben Haddad, 58, and I operate a crusher at a large mine. At the start I check guards, belts and the feed hopper, then keep the rock moving without choking the machine. I like finding the sound of a loose roller before it breaks, though the dust gets into everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nadia does payroll at a bus company, and our children are grown and independent. I earn more than most crusher operators and we have about fourteen months of expenses saved. I have a vocational certificate, several mines are nearby, and I use an AI assistant daily to sort fault logs and find parts in the manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my shift that a tidier fault log is welcome if the guard inspection still happens in person. I already use AI each day to sort the notes, and I catch its mistakes. A clean sentence does not mean a clean conveyor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d expect my crusher hours and higher pay to carry on. Nadia’s payroll job looks steady under a small change, and fourteen months of savings gives us room. I would keep building that buffer because a mine can close for reasons other than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep running the crusher and checking guards before each start. I’d use the AI assistant to draft the handover log and compare every fault with the paper maintenance record. In the first year I’d keep adding two hundred monthly to savings while both wages come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm, with my normal interest in better tools. I would still feel responsible for the person who takes my shift. The household would have time to talk about retirement without a forced date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake have you caught?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The assistant once called a hot bearing a routine vibration note. I wrote the temperature down, stopped the conveyor and called the fitter before another shift ran it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep saving with fourteen months already there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia and I are still paying for the house, and a long shutdown would eat the cushion. Two hundred a month is manageable without relying on our children.

say: I’d welcome **cleaner fault logs** while insisting on physical guard checks.
A tidy AI sentence cannot prove the **conveyor** is safe.
think: My **crusher wage** and Nadia’s payroll work appear steady, giving us room to keep paying down the house.
Fourteen months of savings gives us **retirement room**.
do: Keep operating the **crusher** after guard and belt checks.
Use AI for **handover logs** and check each fault against paper records.
Add **two hundred monthly** to savings while both wages arrive.
feel: **Calm** about work, with interest in reliable tools.
S0.quote: A clean sentence does not mean a clean conveyor.
fieldNote: Ben uses **AI daily** for fault records but once stopped a conveyor after catching a dangerous summary error.
His **higher wage** and fourteen-month cushion allow continued savings while the household pays down its house.

steps.text: Keep operating the crusher after inspecting guards and belts
Use AI for handover logs and verify faults against paper records
Add two hundred monthly to household savings while both wages arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI will alter Nadia’s payroll desk before a robot feeds my crusher. I’d want the bus company to explain its staffing plan, and I’d ask our mine to let operators test any new feed schedule. People should not be priced out of work by a secret timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect paid crusher shifts to continue for now, with other local mines as a fallback. Nadia’s payroll checking could be cut down to one person and software, though, and that would reduce our household income. Fourteen months saved buys a response, not a reason to ignore my partner Nadia’s payroll job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d sit with Nadia this weekend and list which payroll checks her office already automates. At the mine I’d ask to test the new feed scheduling screen against the real hopper limits. During the first year I’d keep running the crusher and take any wrong feed rate to the shift supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about Nadia’s income even while curious about the mine tool. I would not tell her to leave a job she likes because a forecast sounds bad. We would compare her actual roster with our budget each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wrong feed rate do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Too much rock in a short run can jam the hopper and leave people clearing it by hand. I’d show the supervisor the stoppage log before anyone calls that rate efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Nadia welcome your list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She is tired of people outside payroll assuming it is only typing. I’d ask her what changed on her own desk before I made plans for her.

say: I’d say **payroll work** changes before crusher robots arrive.
I’d ask operators to test **feed schedules** against hopper limits.
think: My **crusher shifts** should continue, but Nadia’s payroll hours could shrink.
Our **fourteen-month cushion** gives us time to respond to a cut.
do: List Nadia’s **payroll checks** with her this weekend.
Test the **feed screen** against hopper limits.
Keep running the crusher and report **wrong rates** during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, yet curious about a useful mine tool.
S1.quote: Fourteen months saved buys a response, not a reason to ignore my partner Nadia’s payroll job.
fieldNote: Ben’s own **crusher shifts** look stable in the near term, while Nadia’s payroll checking is directly exposed to AI.
He wants **operator testing** because a wrong feed rate can jam the hopper and put clearing crews at risk.

steps.text: Test the AI feed schedule against actual hopper limits
Keep operating the crusher and report wrong feed rates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers that full thinking AI in 2028 could remove Nadia’s payroll work, and robots able to run the crusher follow around 2031. I would ask both workplaces for actual staffing and machine dates. We need a safety plan and an income plan, not another launch video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when payroll faces the full AI and 63 when crusher robots can do my work. Even fourteen months of savings would not replace two wages for the remaining years we expected to earn. Several nearby mines may be trying the same robot machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask Nadia to request her employer’s staffing plan and I’d get our retirement figures this month. I’d apply for an advertised crushing-plant role at another local mine if ours sets a definite cut date. Through 2029 I’d keep my paid crusher shifts, try any approved robot-feed monitor the mine offers, and postpone the roof terrace project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious, not helpless. The savings give us time to compare job offers and bills, but they cannot manufacture a new payroll post for Nadia. I would push for an honest date before either of us signs an exit paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would monitoring robots be a lasting job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the monitor if it keeps me earning, but a capable robot might need little oversight. I’d treat it as a temporary option until the contract says otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost gets delayed first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roof terrace can wait; the roof itself is sound. I’d tell the builder before we buy materials, and put that cash beside the savings account.

say: I’d ask both employers for **staffing dates** before decisions are forced.
I’d insist on a **crusher safety plan** for capable robots.
think: At **63**, crusher robots could end my higher mine pay.
Nadia may lose **payroll income** sooner, and fourteen months cannot replace two wages for years.
do: Get **retirement figures** and ask for Nadia’s staffing plan.
Apply for a posted **local plant job** after a definite cut date.
Keep paid crusher shifts in **2029**, try the monitor, and delay the terrace.
feel: **Anxious** about two exposed wages, with savings giving us time to act.
S2.quote: Even fourteen months of savings would not replace two wages for the remaining years we expected to earn.
fieldNote: Ben sees **payroll loss** in 2028 as a household risk and **crusher robots** in 2031 as another income threat.
He would try **robot monitoring** for paid work but explicitly doubts that capable machines would need many overseers.

steps.text: Keep operating the crusher for pay through 2029 if shifts remain
Try the approved robot-feed monitor if the mine offers it
Apply for an advertised local crushing-plant job after a cut date
Postpone the roof terrace project before buying materials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets the payroll staff and mine crew make separate plans. Full thinking AI comes in 2031, then crusher robots around 2034, when I would be 66. I would ask our union branch to negotiate real notice and paid retraining places while we are still working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be ready to retire at 66, but Nadia could lose her payroll wage at 63 while we still have house costs. I cannot assume a pension amount without reading the statement. The longer warning gives us space, yet a smaller household income is a real possibility within five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for both retirement statements and set out our house payments with Nadia. I’d continue paid crusher shifts and attend the union branch meeting to vote on notice and paid training terms. In 2032 I’d check whether Nadia still has paid payroll work, then compare that with any mine exit offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about the payroll gap, though less hurried than in the 2028 picture. I could work with five years of numbers and meetings. I would still keep the crusher wage as long as it is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would paid training mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might take a short course if it led to a posted job with paid hours. Training by itself cannot guarantee work once thinking AI and robots can do the tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to help with the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, they have their own households and jobs. Nadia and I have saved enough to plan first, and I would ask the union for fair notice rather than send our bills to them.

say: I’d ask for union **notice terms** and paid training places.
I’d tell coworkers **2031 AI** reaches payroll before 2034 crusher robots.
think: Nadia could lose **payroll pay** while we still have house costs.
At **66**, retirement might work, but the pension amount is unverified.
do: Get both **retirement statements** and list house payments.
Keep paid crusher shifts and vote at the **union meeting**.
Check Nadia’s **2032 payroll income** before comparing exit terms.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with time to make a plan.
S3.quote: Training by itself cannot guarantee work once thinking AI and robots can do the tasks.
fieldNote: Nadia’s possible **2031 payroll loss** keeps this scenario financially live despite a later robot threat to Ben.
Ben backs **paid training places** through union action but doubts that courses alone can secure future work.

steps.text: Keep operating the crusher for pay through 2032 if offered
Attend the union branch meeting and vote on notice and training terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the ten-year warning gives us time to document what a safe feed rate really is. Full thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I would be 68, and crusher robots follow around 2039, when I would be 71. I hope to be retired before robots control that hopper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like to stop before 68 if our pension and savings support it, but I cannot name a date yet. Nadia may also choose to leave payroll before full AI arrives. Our higher mine wage, long cushion and nearby job options make the next few years feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d review our retirement statements with Nadia each winter and keep saving from my mine wages. I’d continue paid crusher shifts while health and the mine allow, and write down the roller and hopper checks for the next operator. In 2037 I’d compare our income with house and living costs before deciding whether to be fully retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about my own job in the near term and thoughtful about the crew that follows me. A decade gives us room to choose rather than gamble. I would want the safety notes used even after I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the safety notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d describe the sound of a failing roller and the feed rate that jams the hopper on wet rock. A new operator should hear a failing crusher roller beside the machine, not just read my log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you simply retire tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings would cover a period, but I have not shown that retirement income covers years of bills. Nadia and I would check the statements before changing both of our work plans.

say: I’d use **ten years** to document safe crusher limits.
I hope to leave paid work before **2039 robots** run the hopper.
think: I want to retire before **68** if the figures support it.
Our **long cushion** and local jobs make the near years feel secure.
do: Review **retirement statements** with Nadia each winter.
Keep paid crusher shifts and save part of **mine wages**.
Compare **2037 income** with house and living costs.
feel: **Calm** about near-term earnings, with care for the next crew.
S4.quote: A new operator should hear a failing crusher roller beside the machine, not just read my log.
fieldNote: Ben expects **2039 robots** after his likely crusher career, with household retirement still subject to pension and bill figures.
He wants **safety knowledge** passed through machine-side teaching, not only a written fault log.

steps.text: Keep operating the crusher for pay while health and work allow
Save part of mine wages while checking retirement statements yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because Nadia’s payroll wage could fall first and crusher robots could cut mine pay at 63. We need real dates, open local jobs and a safety plan before anyone claims the transition is orderly. Fourteen months of savings is time to act, not a second career.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who hears a bearing go wrong when fewer people are beside the crusher. The log can help, but somebody still has to stop the feed. I want the new operators paid enough time to learn that sound.

headlineQuote: Fourteen months of savings is time to act, not a second career.
portrait: Ben, **58**, runs a crusher and uses AI daily for fault notes while checking them against the machine.
His **higher mine pay** and Nadia’s payroll wage support fourteen months of expenses saved.
He tests **new tools early** and seeks union terms for notice and paid training.
Fast AI threatens **Nadia’s pay** before capable robots reach his crusher around 2031.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries Ben most because payroll income may fall before crusher robots end his mine wages at 63.
whatWouldHelp: Real **staffing dates**, local vacancies and a crusher safety plan would help them respond.
